prompt: How many α-amino acids does the section say are each degraded through their own unique pathway?
explanation: Protein catabolism is complex because each of the 20 α-amino acids is degraded through its own unique pathway.

prompt: What is the general scheme for amino acid catabolism?

choices.text: The amino group leaves as ammonia (then urea), and the carbon skeleton enters the citric acid cycle
The amino acid is converted directly into glucose, which is broken down in glycolysis
choices.why: The section's scheme removes the amino group first and sends the carbon skeleton to the citric acid cycle.

choices.text: The amino acid is hydrolyzed to an amide, which is excreted
choices.why: Amide hydrolysis happens in digestion. Amino acids lose their amino group as ammonia.

choices.text: The carboxyl group is removed as CO2, and the amine is oxidized to a nitrile
choices.why: The section describes deamination, not decarboxylation.

explanation: Each amino acid has its own pathway, but in general (1) the α amino group is removed as ammonia by deamination, (2) the ammonia is converted into urea, and (3) the carbon skeleton is converted into a compound that enters the citric acid cycle.

prompt: After deamination, what kind of compound is the remaining amino acid carbon skeleton usually?

choices.text: An α-keto acid
An α-hydroxy acid
choices.why: The amino group is replaced by a keto group, not a hydroxyl.

choices.text: A fatty acid
choices.why: The skeleton keeps its α carbon oxidized as a ketone; it is an α-keto acid.

choices.text: An amide
choices.why: The nitrogen is removed in deamination, so no amide is left.

explanation: The remaining amino acid carbon skeleton is usually an α-keto acid, which is converted into a compound that enters the citric acid cycle.

prompt: In amino acid catabolism, what is the ammonia removed by deamination converted into?

choices.text: Urea
Glutamine
choices.why: The section's general scheme says the ammonia is converted into urea.

choices.text: Nitrate
choices.why: Nitrate isn't mentioned. Ammonia is converted into urea.

choices.text: Uric acid
choices.why: The section's scheme says urea.

explanation: Step (2) of the general scheme: the ammonia removed from the α amino group is converted into urea.

prompt: In a transamination, the –NH2 group of an amino acid is exchanged with the keto group of α-ketoglutarate. What are the products?

choices.text: A new α-keto acid plus glutamate
A new α-keto acid plus ammonia
choices.why: In transamination the amino group isn't released as ammonia; it is transferred to α-ketoglutarate, giving glutamate.

choices.text: An α-hydroxy acid plus glutamate
choices.why: The amino acid becomes an α-keto acid, not a hydroxy acid.

choices.text: A new amino acid plus pyruvate
choices.why: α-Ketoglutarate is the keto acid used, so it becomes glutamate, not pyruvate.

explanation: Deamination is usually accomplished by transamination: the –NH2 group of the amino acid is exchanged with the keto group of α-ketoglutarate, forming a new α-keto acid plus glutamate.

prompt: Which coenzyme takes part in transamination, catalyzed by aminotransferases?

choices.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), a derivative of pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
Thiamin diphosphate (TPP), a derivative of vitamin B1
choices.why: TPP is used in the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA.

choices.text: Biotin
choices.why: Biotin carries CO2 in carboxylations.

choices.text: Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)
choices.why: FAD is an oxidizing coenzyme used in β-oxidation and the citric acid cycle.

explanation: Transamination occurs in two parts, is catalyzed by aminotransferases, and involves the coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), a derivative of pyridoxine (vitamin B6). The aminotransferases differ in specificity, but the mechanism is the same.

prompt: How is pyridoxal phosphate bonded to the aminotransferase before the amino acid arrives?

choices.text: By an imine linkage between a lysine side-chain –NH2 group and the PLP aldehyde group
By a thioester linkage to a cysteine residue
choices.why: Thioesters link acyl groups to sulfur. PLP is held by an imine to lysine.

choices.text: By an ester linkage to a serine –OH
choices.why: That describes how phosphopantetheine attaches to ACP. PLP is bonded to lysine as an imine.

choices.text: By an amide bond between PLP's phosphate and a histidine
choices.why: The link is an imine between the PLP aldehyde and lysine.

explanation: PLP is covalently bonded to the aminotransferase by an imine linkage between the side-chain –NH2 group of a lysine residue and the PLP aldehyde group.

prompt: What happens in step 1 of transamination, transimination?

choices.text: The amino acid –NH2 adds to the C=N bond of the PLP–enzyme imine, and the enzyme's lysine amino group is expelled
Water adds to the PLP imine and PMP is expelled
choices.why: That is the hydrolysis at the end of the first part of transamination.

choices.text: The enzyme lysine deprotonates the α position of the amino acid
choices.why: That deprotonation is the tautomerization step, step 2.

choices.text: PMP reacts with α-ketoglutarate to give glutamate
choices.why: That is the regeneration of PLP, the second part of transamination.

explanation: In transimination, the amino acid –NH2 group adds to the C=N bond of the PLP imine, much as an amine adds to a ketone or aldehyde C=O. The protonated diamine intermediate undergoes proton transfer and expels the enzyme's lysine amino group, giving a PLP–amino acid imine.

prompt: In step 2 of transamination, the C=N bond tautomerizes. Which group deprotonates the acidic α position of the amino acid, and what acts as the electron acceptor?

choices.text: The lysine residue expelled in step 1; the protonated pyridine ring of PLP
A histidine residue; NAD+
choices.why: No NAD+ is involved. The base is the freed lysine, and the electron acceptor is the PLP pyridine ring.

choices.text: Water; the carboxylate group of the amino acid
choices.why: The base is the enzyme's lysine, and the pyridine ring of PLP accepts the electrons.

choices.text: The PLP phosphate group; a Mg^2+ ion
choices.why: The section names the lysine as the base and the protonated pyridine ring as the electron acceptor.

explanation: The basic lysine residue that was expelled during transimination deprotonates the α position, with the protonated pyridine ring of PLP acting as the electron acceptor. Reprotonation on the carbon next to the ring gives the imine of an α-keto acid with pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP).

prompt: What does hydrolysis of the PMP–α-keto acid imine give, completing the first part of transamination?

choices.text: An α-keto acid plus pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP)
An α-amino acid plus pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
choices.why: Those are the starting materials of the first part.

choices.text: Glutamate plus PLP
choices.why: Glutamate and PLP are the products of the second part, the regeneration of PLP.

choices.text: Ammonia plus an α-keto acid
choices.why: The nitrogen stays on the coenzyme as PMP; it isn't released as ammonia.

explanation: Hydrolysis of the PMP–α-keto acid imine, the reverse of imine formation, occurs by nucleophilic addition of water, proton transfer and expulsion of PMP, giving the α-keto acid plus pyridoxamine phosphate.

prompt: How is PLP regenerated from PMP to complete the catalytic cycle?

choices.text: By another transamination, usually with α-ketoglutarate, giving PLP plus glutamate by the exact reverse mechanism
By oxidation of PMP with NAD+
choices.why: No oxidizing coenzyme is used. PMP gives its amino group to α-ketoglutarate.

choices.text: By hydrolysis of PMP to release ammonia
choices.why: The amino group is passed to an α-keto acid, giving glutamate, not ammonia.

choices.text: By reaction of PMP with a second amino acid
choices.why: PMP already carries the amino group. It must react with an α-keto acid, usually α-ketoglutarate.

explanation: PMP reacts with an α-keto acid, usually α-ketoglutarate, in another transamination whose mechanism is the exact reverse of the first part: imine formation, tautomerization to a PLP–glutamate imine, then transimination with the enzyme's lysine to give the PLP–enzyme imine plus glutamate.

prompt: In how many parts does the overall transamination process occur?
explanation: Transamination occurs in two parts: first the α-amino acid and PLP give an α-keto acid plus PMP; then PMP and α-ketoglutarate give PLP plus glutamate.

prompt: Leucine is (CH3)2CHCH2CH(NH2)CO2H in its neutral form. What α-keto acid (as its anion) is formed when leucine undergoes transamination?

choices.text: (CH3)2CHCH2COCO2−
(CH3)2CHCH2CH(OH)CO2−
choices.why: Transamination replaces the amino group with a keto group, not a hydroxyl group.

choices.text: (CH3)2CHCOCO2−
choices.why: That has lost a CH2 group. The carbon skeleton is unchanged; only the α carbon changes.

choices.text: (CH3)2CHCH2CH2CO2−
choices.why: The α carbon becomes a C=O, not a CH2.

explanation: In transamination the α –NH2 (with the α hydrogen) is replaced by a keto group while the carbon skeleton stays the same, so leucine gives (CH3)2CHCH2COCO2− (Exercise 29.9.2).

prompt: Alanine is CH3CH(NH2)CO2H in its neutral form. What α-keto acid anion does transamination of alanine give?

choices.text: Pyruvate, CH3COCO2−
Lactate, CH3CH(OH)CO2−
choices.why: Transamination makes a keto group at the α carbon, not an alcohol.

choices.text: Acetate, CH3CO2−
choices.why: No carbon is lost; the three-carbon skeleton is kept.

choices.text: α-Ketoglutarate
choices.why: α-Ketoglutarate is the amino group acceptor. It has five carbons, not three.

explanation: Replacing the α amino group of alanine with a keto group gives CH3COCO2−, pyruvate, keeping the same three-carbon skeleton. This fits the section's list of compounds that amino acid skeletons are converted into.

prompt: The α-keto acid H2NCOCH2COCO2− is formed by transamination of which amino acid?

choices.text: Asparagine, H2NCOCH2CH(NH2)CO2H
Aspartic acid, HO2CCH2CH(NH2)CO2H
choices.why: Aspartic acid has a side-chain carboxylic acid, not the side-chain amide (H2NCO–) in this keto acid.

choices.text: Glutamine, H2NCOCH2CH2CH(NH2)CO2H
choices.why: Glutamine has one more CH2 group in its side chain.

choices.text: Alanine, CH3CH(NH2)CO2H
choices.why: Alanine gives pyruvate, CH3COCO2−, which has no side-chain amide.

explanation: Transamination changes only the α carbon, turning CH(NH2) into C=O. Putting the amino group back on H2NCOCH2COCO2− gives H2NCOCH2CH(NH2)CO2H, asparagine (Exercise 29.9.3).
